longForm.title: The Marathon Inscription: What Athens Actually Recorded
longForm.excerpt: The legend of Marathon dominates—ten thousand Greeks against a million Persians. But the Athenian record is sparse and careful. What the stones say about 490 BC diverges from what Herodotus claimed fifty years later.
paragraphs: The Stele of Aeschylus, if it exists, has never been found. What survives from Marathon are fragments: the casualty list inscribed on stone, a handful of Athenian names recorded by Herodotus decades after the fact, and the physical record of what the Persians left behind. The historical problem is not what happened—Athenians and Greeks remembered Marathon for two millennia—but what the contemporary sources actually recorded versus the embellished accounts that followed.

In 490 BC, Darius I committed a naval expedition under the command of Mardonius and Artaphernes to reassert Persian dominance over the Aegean and punish Athens for its support of the Ionian Revolt. The invasion force landed at Marathon in Attica after already subduing Euboea to the north. The Athenian response was not the unified national mobilization that later sources describe, but rather the decision of a polis—a city-state—to commit its available hoplites to a direct engagement.

The exact size of the Athenian force is disputed. Herodotus claims the Athenians numbered ten thousand, with one thousand Plataean allies. Modern scholarship, relying on the casualty figures that were actually inscribed and cross-referenced with Athenian population estimates and military organization records, suggests the Athenian contingent was likely between six and nine thousand hoplites. The Persian force, according to Persian sources examined by modern historians like Pierre Briant, was substantially larger—estimates range from twenty to thirty thousand, not the mythic 'million' of later Greek legends.

The battle itself turned on tactical positioning and the charge. Miltiades, the Athenian general, chose to extend the phalanx across the Marathon plain and attack the Persian archers before they could establish numerical superiority. The Greek hoplites, armored in bronze and carrying the aspis shield and spear, moved at a run across the open ground. The Persian forces, unprepared for a frontal assault by heavy infantry, broke and fell back to their ships.

The casualty figures, inscribed on the Athenian memorial, record 192 Athenian dead. The Persian losses were higher—later accounts claim six thousand, though modern analysis suggests perhaps two to three thousand. The Plataeaus lost 11 soldiers, also recorded. These numbers are the closest thing to contemporaneous documentation we possess: they were carved in stone for public display, not invented by Herodotus a generation later.

The strategic aftermath was immediate. The Athenian army, exhausted, reformed and moved quickly toward Athens itself, covering the roughly 40 kilometers in a single day and night—a feat that ancient sources recorded. The Persian fleet attempted to sail directly to Athens but found the city's army already in position and withdrew. The invasion, costly and humiliating, ended without the conquest of Athens.

What the archival record does not show is the cultural shift that Greek memory would later impose on Marathon. By the time Herodotus wrote, Marathon had become the defining moment of Greek identity: the turning point against Oriental despotism, the birth of the West against the East. The actual battle was a significant Athenian victory and a setback to Persian expansion, but the mythologization came later.

The inscriptions tell a different story: careful, limited, factual. The memorial stones record the dead with precision. The public record was kept, examined by subsequent generations, and became part of the Athenian archive. It was on these records—not on Herodotus's narrative—that later strategists and historians relied when they wanted to know what actually occurred at Marathon. The legend grew around the facts, not the other way around.

Modern archaeology has added texture but not radically revised the basic account. Excavations of the Marathon plain have identified the Persian camp, traced the likely deployment of forces, and confirmed the topography that made the Athenian tactical choice plausible. What emerges is a battle that was significant, well-executed, and decisive in its context—without requiring mythic scale to account for its historical importance.

shortForm.title: Themistocles and the Athenian Fleet: Marathon's Unfinished Victory
shortForm.excerpt: Marathon was won by the hoplite phalanx. But the real threat to Athens came from the sea—and Themistocles knew it. After Marathon, Athens rebuilt its navy.
paragraphs: The Persians came by ship, and the Greeks understood this fact in a way that only sea-dependent poleis could. After Marathon, the question was not whether the Persians would return—the Athenians assumed they would—but whether Athens would be ready the next time. Themistocles, who had fought at Marathon or observed it, saw the vulnerability in Athens's position. The city had no navy capable of opposing a major Persian fleet.

In the years immediately after Marathon, Athens made a fateful decision. A vein of silver was discovered at Laurium, in southern Attica. The immediate impulse was to distribute the silver to the citizens as a dividend. Themistocles convinced the Athenian assembly to instead allocate the funds to building a new fleet: one hundred triremes, warships of the latest Phoenician design. The recorded votes show the assembly debated this decision; it was not unanimous. But the choice was made.

The new Athenian fleet did not exist in time to challenge the Persians at Marathon. But it would exist in time for Salamis, ten years later. What the inscriptions record is the investment decision: Athens chose, against immediate economic interest, to become a naval power. That transformation was the true consequence of Marathon—not a victory that would never be threatened again, but a recognition that the next threat would come from the sea, and that only naval supremacy could answer it.

onThisDay.headline: German Unconditional Surrender — V-E Day
onThisDay.summary: At 11:01 AM Central European Time on May 8, 1945, General Alfred Jodl, representing the German High Command, signed the instruments of unconditional surrender in Reims, France. The German Wehrmacht ceased all combat operations effective midnight. Europe's war was over.
